_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 10 Light and Shadows. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the five parts of LESSON[lecture] in content/lesson-10.py in order (three kinds of material; a shadow; big and small shadows; light into the eye; what people used to think), with the lesson's ask step as its own chapter after the experiment, where the lesson puts it. The pictures are the lesson's own: its light tester (ART.sim lightThrough, with window glass, tracing paper and a book, and the sort step's three bin pictures beside it), its demo's torch, hand and wall, and its shadow-size experiment (ART.sim shadowSize, the three positions its buttons step through).
title: Light and Shadows
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Investigate how light can pass through some materials and is blocked by others, and use the terms transparent, translucent and opaque.
Know that shadows are formed when light from a source is blocked by an object.
Investigate how the size of a shadow is affected by the position of the object and the position of the light source.
Use observations and tests to sort, group and classify objects.
Make a prediction describing some possible outcomes of an enquiry.
Make a conclusion from results and relate it to the scientific question being investigated.
Ask scientific questions that can be investigated.
Talk about how some of the scientific knowledge and thinking now was different in the past.

beats.say: Light goes through some things, and is blocked by others.
Where the light is blocked, you get a dark shape: a shadow.
Shine a torch at window glass. The light goes straight through.
The wall behind is bright. Glass is transparent: you see clearly.
Now tracing paper. Some light gets through, but it is blurred.
Tracing paper is translucent. You see light, but no clear shapes.
Now a book. No light gets through at all. A book is opaque.
Test each material, then sort it: transparent, translucent or opaque.
A torch shines on a wall. The wall is bright.
Put your hand in the way. Your hand is opaque, so it blocks the light.
Where the light is blocked, the wall stays dark.
That dark shape is a shadow. It is the shape of your hand.
A shadow does not come out of your hand. It is where light cannot reach.
Switch the torch off. No light, nothing to block, so no shadow.
Here is a torch, a toy and a wall.
Predict first. Will its shadow get bigger, get smaller, or stay the same?
Keep the torch and the wall still. Move only the toy.

at.keep: Keep the torch and the wall still

beats.say: Move the toy towards the torch, and its shadow grows.

at.move: Move the toy towards the torch

beats.say: Move it towards the wall, and its shadow shrinks.
The toy has not changed. Where it is has changed, and that changes how much light it blocks.
A good scientific question can be tested.
Does the shadow get bigger if the torch moves further away?
Move only the torch back, and look. The shadow gets smaller.
A torch and the Sun are light sources. They make their own light.
Light from a source bounces off things and goes into your eye.
That is how you see. In a completely dark room, you see nothing.
However hard you look, there is no light to see by.
Long ago, some people thought eyes sent out beams to see with.
It seemed sensible. But it was wrong.
Testing showed light comes from a source into the eye.
Science changes when people test their ideas.
Transparent lets light through, translucent lets some, opaque lets none.
A shadow forms where something opaque blocks the light.
Nearer the light source, bigger shadow. Nearer the wall, smaller.
You see when light goes into your eye. Testing ideas changes science.
